title: DSLs, Operators, Contracts
scopeHtml: Scope: operator conventions, infix functions, lambdas with receiver in type-safe builders, @DslMarker, Gradle Kotlin DSL and Compose as real-world DSLs, and Kotlin contracts (callsInPlace, returns implies) with their opt-in status.

questions.promptHtml: What does the operator keyword do in Kotlin, and which operators can you overload?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It checks whether you know that Kotlin operators are only syntax that maps to named functions, and that you know the fixed list instead of assuming you can invent operators like in Scala or Haskell.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: In Kotlin an operator is syntax sugar for a call to a function with a fixed name. a + b compiles to a.plus(b), a[i] to a.get(i), x in c to c.contains(x). You mark that function operator to say you meant it to be used that way. The set of operators is closed: you can't create new symbols, change precedence, or overload ===, && or ||. The function can be a member or an extension, so you can add operators to types you don't own.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The compiler has a fixed table that maps each operator to a function name. If it finds a function with the right name and signature marked operator (member or extension in scope), it rewrites the expression to a call to it. There's no runtime dispatch beyond what the function call itself does.

Syntax Translates to Notes
+a, -a, !a a.unaryPlus(), a.unaryMinus(), a.not()
a++, a-- a.inc(), a.dec() Must return a value; the compiler reassigns a. Don't mutate inside.
a + b, -, *, /, % plus, minus, times, div, rem rem replaced the older mod operator name (introduced in Kotlin 1.1)
a..b, a..<b a.rangeTo(b), a.rangeUntil(b) ..< operator is stable since Kotlin 1.9
a in b, a !in b b.contains(a), !b.contains(a) Note the receiver is the right side
a[i], a[i, j] a.get(i), a.get(i, j) Any number of indices, any types
a[i] = v a.set(i, v)
a(x) a.invoke(x)
a += b a.plusAssign(b) or a = a + b Resolution rules matter (see Q239)
a == b a?.equals(b) ?: (b === null) equals is an override of Any.equals, already operator
a < b, >, <=, >= a.compareTo(b) < 0 etc. compareTo must return Int
val (x, y) = p p.component1(), p.component2()
for (x in c) c.iterator(), hasNext(), next() All three need operator
val x by d getValue/setValue/provideDelegate Delegation is covered in the properties chunk

What you cannot do:

  • Define new symbols (<=>, |>), change precedence or associativity.
  • Overload ===, !==, &&, ||, ?:, ?., !! or =.
  • Overload == with a parameter type other than Any?. You only override equals(other: Any?).

The operator modifier is required. A plain fun plus(...) won't work with +. This is deliberate: it stops a method that happens to be called get or contains from silently becoming an operator. Java methods with matching names and signatures are the exception. They're treated as operators automatically, which is why map[key] works on java.util.HashMap.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
data class Money(val cents: Long, val currency: String) : Comparable<Money> {
    operator fun plus(other: Money): Money {
        require(currency == other.currency) { "Currency mismatch: $currency vs ${other.currency}" }
        return Money(cents + other.cents, currency)
    }
    operator fun times(factor: Int): Money = Money(cents * factor, currency)
    operator fun unaryMinus(): Money = Money(-cents, currency)
    override fun compareTo(other: Money): Int {
        require(currency == other.currency)
        return cents.compareTo(other.cents)
    }
}

// Extension operator on a type you do not own
operator fun Money.div(parts: Int): Money = Money(cents / parts, currency)

fun demo() {
    val a = Money(1_000, "INR")
    val b = Money(250, "INR")
    val total = a + b * 2          // precedence of * over + is preserved: 1500
    val isBigger = a > b           // a.compareTo(b) > 0
    val share = total / 3          // extension operator
    println("$total $isBigger $share ${-a}")
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Writing inc() so that it mutates this and returns this. Then val old = a++ gives old and a as the same mutated object. inc has to return a new value.
  • Overloading operators whose meaning isn't obvious (* on two Users). Use operators only where the maths or collection meaning is obvious. Otherwise use a named function.
  • Assuming a in b calls a function on a. It's b.contains(a), so the extension goes on the container type.
  • Treating compareTo as a full ordering while equals disagrees with it. Then a <= b && a >= b is true but a != b, which breaks sorted sets.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can an operator be an extension function? → Yes. A member wins if both exist. Extensions are resolved statically on the declared type.
  2. Why does map[key] work on Java's HashMap without operator? → Java methods with the right name and shape are treated as operators automatically.
  3. Do operators cost anything at runtime? → No more than the call. a + b is just a.plus(b). For primitives the compiler emits the JVM instruction directly. The cost is whatever your function allocates, for example a new object per plus.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer lists plus and get. A senior also says the set is closed and maps to fixed names, explains that == is null-safe and goes through equals, that in dispatches on the right-hand side, that inc must not mutate, and treats operator overloading as an API-readability decision with allocation costs.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An operator fun plus on a Money type that silently added amounts in different currencies (no require check) produced wrong cart totals for users with cross-currency promos. The fix was a single require in the operator.

questions.promptHtml: What is an infix function, what rules does it have to follow, and where does its precedence sit?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Infix shows up all over DSLs and test libraries (to, shouldBe, until, and, shl). Interviewers want to know you understand the precedence trap and the hidden Pair allocation behind to.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: An infix function is a member or extension function with exactly one parameter, marked infix, so you can call it without the dot and parentheses: a to b instead of a.to(b). The parameter can't be vararg or have a default value. Infix calls bind more loosely than arithmetic, range and type casts, but more tightly than elvis, in/is, comparison and equality. So 1 shl 2 + 3 is 1 shl 5. The best-known one is to, and it allocates a Pair on every call.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Rules:

  • Must be a member function or an extension function. It has to have a receiver, so a top-level non-extension function can't be infix.
  • Exactly one parameter, no vararg, no default value.
  • Inside a class you can't call your own infix function without a receiver: this foo x works, foo x doesn't.

Precedence (high to low, simplified):

postfix (a++, a.b, a?.b, a!!)
prefix  (-a, !a, ++a)
type RHS (:, as, as?)
multiplicative (*, /, %)
additive (+, -)
range (.., ..<)
INFIX FUNCTION CALL      <- here
elvis (?:)
named checks (in, !in, is, !is)
comparison (<, >, <=, >=)
equality (==, !=)
&&
||

Consequences:

  • 1 shl 2 + 3 is 1 shl (2 + 3) = 32, not (1 shl 2) + 3 = 7. Bit operations in Kotlin are infix functions, not real operators, so they don't follow C/Java precedence.
  • x to y ?: z is (x to y) ?: z.
  • a until b step 2 is evaluated left to right as (a until b) step 2, because infix calls are left-associative.

Bytecode: infix changes nothing at runtime. a to b compiles to the call TuplesKt.to(a, b), and that call allocates a Pair. mapOf("a" to 1, "b" to 2) therefore allocates two Pairs, a vararg array, a LinkedHashMap and its entries. That's fine in config code, but wasteful inside onDraw or a tight loop.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
infix fun Int.percentOf(total: Int): Int = this * total / 100

class Version(val major: Int, val minor: Int) {
    infix fun isAtLeast(other: Version): Boolean =
        major > other.major || (major == other.major && minor >= other.minor)

    fun check(min: Version) = this isAtLeast min   // `isAtLeast min` alone does not compile
}

fun precedence() {
    val a = 1 shl 2 + 3        // 32, NOT 7
    val b = (1 shl 2) + 3      // 7, parenthesise bit ops
    val c = 20 percentOf 50 + 50  // 20 percentOf 100 = 20
    println("$a $b $c")
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Porting Java bit-manipulation code like flags shl 2 or mask + 1 without parentheses. It gives different results silently.
  • Building large maps with to in hot paths. Each pair is a heap object.
  • Making a function infix when it reads badly. user infix order is not clearer than user.place(order). Infix fits symmetric relations and DSL words (shouldBe, and, until).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can an infix function be generic or an extension on a nullable type? → Yes to both. infix fun <A, B> A.to(that: B): Pair<A, B> is generic. An extension on T? also works.
  2. How do you avoid the Pair allocation in a map built inside a loop? → Use HashMap(capacity) and put, or buildMap { put(k, v) }. Both skip the Pair objects.
  3. Why are and/or/shl infix functions instead of operators? → Kotlin keeps a small operator set. Bitwise ops are rare enough that a readable name was chosen over C symbols. For Int/Long they're intrinsics, so the JVM still emits ishl, iand and so on.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "you can call it without a dot". A senior also states the single-parameter rules, gives the precedence position with the shl example, points out that to allocates, and gives a judgment on when infix helps readability.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A checksum ported from Java (crc shl 8 xor table[idx] and 0xFF) produced different values from the server for some payloads because of infix precedence. The bug only showed up as signature-mismatch 4xx errors for a slice of users.

questions.subtopic: Indexed access, contains, ranges, iterator conventions
questions.promptHtml: How do get/set, contains, rangeTo/rangeUntil and the iterator convention work? Show how you'd make a custom type usable with [], in and for.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: These conventions are how collections and grids feel "built in". The interviewer checks that you know the exact shape of each, including that for needs no interface and that in on primitive ranges doesn't allocate.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: a[i, j] calls operator fun get(i, j), which can take any number of parameters of any types. a[i] = v calls set(i, v), with the value as the last parameter. x in c calls c.contains(x). a..b and a..<b call rangeTo and rangeUntil. A for loop only needs an operator fun iterator() whose return type has operator fun hasNext(): Boolean and operator fun next(). You don't need to implement Iterable, and an extension works too. For integer ranges the compiler optimises for (i in 0 until n) and x in 0..10 into plain comparisons with no range object.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• get/set: Multiple indices are allowed, for example grid[row, col]. set takes the indices first and the new value last. Compound assignment a[i] += 1 becomes a.set(i, a.get(i).plus(1)), or a.get(i).plusAssign(1) if that resolves (see Q239).
  • contains: It must return Boolean. !in negates it. It's also used in when (x) { in range -> ... }.
  • rangeTo / rangeUntil: They return whatever you want, usually a ClosedRange<T> or OpenEndRange<T>. For any Comparable<T> the stdlib already provides rangeTo, so dateA..dateB gives you a ClosedRange<LocalDate> and d in dateA..dateB works without writing anything. rangeUntil and ..< became stable in Kotlin 1.9.
  • iterator convention: The compiler lowers it like this:
for (x in c) body
  =>
val it = c.iterator()
while (it.hasNext()) { val x = it.next(); body }

Because it's a convention and not an interface, you can make a third-party class iterable with an extension operator fun Foo.iterator(). Android's ViewGroup already gets children and iterator() extensions from androidx.core.view.

  • Intrinsics: for (i in 0 until n), for (i in a..b step 2), for (i in array.indices) and x in 0..10 on Int/Long/Char compile to index loops or two comparisons. A range stored in a variable (val r = 0..n; x in r) or a custom range type is a real object, and contains is a real call. Check the bytecode (Tools > Kotlin > Show Kotlin Bytecode) when it matters.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class Grid<T>(val rows: Int, val cols: Int, init: (Int, Int) -> T) {
    private val cells: MutableList<T> = MutableList(rows * cols) { init(it / cols, it % cols) }

    operator fun get(r: Int, c: Int): T = cells[index(r, c)]
    operator fun set(r: Int, c: Int, value: T) { cells[index(r, c)] = value }
    operator fun contains(value: T): Boolean = value in cells
    operator fun iterator(): Iterator<T> = cells.iterator()

    private fun index(r: Int, c: Int): Int {
        require(r in 0 until rows && c in 0 until cols) { "($r,$c) out of $rows x $cols" }
        return r * cols + c
    }
}

// Extension makes a type you do not own usable in `for`
operator fun android.database.Cursor.iterator(): Iterator<android.database.Cursor> =
    object : Iterator<android.database.Cursor> {
        override fun hasNext() = position < count - 1
        override fun next(): android.database.Cursor {
            if (!moveToNext()) throw NoSuchElementException()
            return this@iterator
        }
    }

fun demo() {
    val g = Grid(3, 3) { r, c -> r * 3 + c }
    g[1, 1] = 42
    g[0, 0] += 1                 // get, plus, set
    println(42 in g)             // g.contains(42)
    for (cell in g) print(cell)  // g.iterator()
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking for requires Iterable. It doesn't. Only the operator functions are needed.
  • Writing operator fun get that silently returns a default for out-of-range indices. Callers expect [] to fail fast the way lists do. Offer getOrNull separately.
  • Storing a range in a val inside a hot loop and assuming it's still optimised. It's a real IntRange object, and contains is a call. That's usually harmless, but it isn't free.
  • A Cursor iterator that returns the same mutable cursor each time. Collecting it with toList() gives N references to one object pointing at the last row. That's a real trap in this example, so document it or map each row immediately.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can get take a String index? → Yes. Any types and any number of parameters, for example json["user", "name"].
  2. How is a[i] += 1 resolved? → If get(i) returns a type with plusAssign, that's called. Otherwise it's set(i, get(i) + 1).
  3. Why does x in 0..n not allocate but x in someRange might? → The compiler recognises a literal range of primitives in an in or for and emits comparisons. A range held in a variable is an object, so contains is a virtual call. The JIT may still inline it, but the object exists.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer knows get/set. A senior knows for is a convention, not an interface, explains how a[i] += 1 expands, mentions that Comparable gets rangeTo for free, and knows which range forms are intrinsified and how to check in bytecode.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A Cursor.iterator() extension like the one above, followed by .toList(), rendered every row of a contacts list as the last contact. The bug was invisible in a test with a single row.

questions.promptHtml: What does a += b compile to? Why can var list = mutableListOf<Int>(); list += 1 fail to compile, and how do compareTo and == work as operators?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It's the most common operator ambiguity in real code. It also shows whether you understand mutation versus reassignment, which matters for StateFlow and Compose state.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: For a += b the compiler looks for plusAssign and for plus. If only plusAssign applies, it mutates in place. If only plus applies and a is a var, it becomes a = a + b, which creates a new object and reassigns. If both apply and a is a var, the compiler reports an "assignment operators ambiguity" error, because it can't know whether you meant to mutate or reassign. MutableList has both plus (returns a new list) and plusAssign (adds in place), so var plus MutableList is ambiguous. Use val with a mutable list, or var with a read-only List. < and the other comparisons go through compareTo(...) < 0. == goes through equals with a built-in null check, and === can't be overloaded.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Resolution for a += b:

plusAssign applicable?   plus applicable & a is var?   result
------------------------------------------------------------------
yes                      no                            a.plusAssign(b)   (must return Unit)
no                       yes                           a = a.plus(b)     (result type must fit a's type)
yes                      yes                           COMPILE ERROR: ambiguity
no                       no                            COMPILE ERROR

Two correct patterns:

  • val items = mutableListOf<Int>(); items += 1 mutates the same list object.
  • var items = listOf<Int>(); items += 1 builds a new list and reassigns. This is the pattern you want for StateFlow and Compose state, because the reference changes and observers notice.

Why it matters on Android: _state.value.items += x, or mutating a MutableList that is already inside a StateFlow, changes the contents but not the reference. StateFlow compares by equals, and here the same instance compares equal to itself, so nothing is emitted. That's the "mutating a list inside StateFlow" bug. The reactive-state chunk covers it in depth; operators are just how it's written.

Comparison: a < b becomes a.compareTo(b) < 0. Implementing Comparable<T> gives you <, >, <= and >=, plus coerceIn, rangeTo and maxOf from the stdlib. For floating point, == on statically typed Double follows IEEE 754 (-0.0 == 0.0 is true, NaN == NaN is false). When the static type is Any or Comparable, equals semantics apply instead (NaN equals itself, -0.0 < 0.0). That difference is a known gotcha.

Equality: a == b becomes a?.equals(b) ?: (b === null). You can't pick a different parameter type. equals(other: Money) is an overload, not an override, and == won't call it.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
fun ambiguity() {
    var broken = mutableListOf(1, 2)
    // broken += 3            // ERROR: Assignment operators ambiguity (plus vs plusAssign)

    val inPlace = mutableListOf(1, 2)
    inPlace += 3              // plusAssign, same object

    var immutable = listOf(1, 2)
    immutable += 3            // immutable = immutable + 3, new object
}

class Counter(var value: Int) {
    operator fun plusAssign(delta: Int) { value += delta }  // must return Unit
}

// StateFlow: reassign, do not mutate
data class UiState(val items: List<String> = emptyList())
val state = kotlinx.coroutines.flow.MutableStateFlow(UiState())
fun add(item: String) {
    state.value = state.value.copy(items = state.value.items + item) // new list -> emits
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "Fixing" the ambiguity error by writing list.add(x) on a var MutableList, which hides the real design question of whether the variable should be reassigned at all.
  • Defining both plus and plusAssign on your own mutable type, which gives every var caller an ambiguity error.
  • Expecting equals(other: MyType) to be used by ==. It must be override fun equals(other: Any?).
  • Mixing statically typed Double comparisons with generic Comparable sorting and getting different answers for NaN/-0.0.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can plusAssign return a value? → No. It must return Unit, or the compiler rejects it as an assignment operator.
  2. What happens with a += b when a is a val and only plus exists? → Compile error, because reassignment isn't possible.
  3. Why does (0.0 / 0.0) == (0.0 / 0.0) print false but listOf(Double.NaN).contains(Double.NaN) print true? → Statically typed Double == uses IEEE 754. Collection lookup goes through boxed equals, which treats NaN as equal to itself.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "+= is plus then assign". A senior gives the four-way resolution table, explains why var plus a mutable collection is ambiguous, connects it to reference-equality in StateFlow and Compose, and knows the IEEE versus equals difference for floating point.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team "fixed" a non-updating screen by switching val items: MutableList in a state holder to var plus +=, got the ambiguity error, then used .add(). The screen still didn't update, because the reference never changed. The real fix was an immutable List with reassignment.

questions.promptHtml: How do type-safe builders work in Kotlin? Explain lambdas with receiver, how they compile, and walk me through building a small DSL.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Every Kotlin DSL (Gradle, Ktor routing, Compose scopes, buildList, buildString) rests on this one mechanism. Seniors are expected to design such APIs, not just use them.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A lambda with receiver has the type T.() -> R. Inside it, this is a T, so you can call T's members without a qualifier. A builder function creates a T, runs the lambda on it, and returns the result. That's the whole pattern: fun html(block: HTML.() -> Unit) = HTML().apply(block). Nesting comes from member functions that take their own receiver lambdas. On the JVM, T.() -> R is just a Function1<T, R> with the receiver passed as the first argument. If the builder is inline, the lambda is inlined and costs nothing.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Mechanism:

type:     HTML.() -> Unit          (function type with receiver)
JVM:      Function1<HTML, Unit>    (receiver = first argument)
call:     block(html)  or  html.block()   both legal
inside:   this: HTML  -> body(), head() resolve as this.body(), this.head()
  • T.() -> R and (T) -> R are interchangeable as values. You can pass one where the other is expected. The difference only affects how the lambda's body resolves names.
  • Implicit receiver resolution: inside nested lambdas, every enclosing receiver is in scope, innermost first. That makes it convenient, and it's also the source of the bug @DslMarker fixes (Q241).
  • Type safety comes from the receiver type. row {} exists only on TableBuilder, so calling it inside html {} directly won't compile. The structure of the document is enforced by which types expose which functions.
  • Builder inference: stdlib functions like buildList { add(1) } infer List<Int> from calls inside the lambda. That's builder type inference, stable since Kotlin 1.7.

Designing a small DSL, step by step:

  1. Model the output as plain immutable data (Request, Screen, Route).
  2. Create mutable builder classes that only exist during construction.
  3. Give each builder a member function per child, each taking ChildBuilder.() -> Unit.
  4. Provide one top-level entry function that builds, validates and returns the immutable result.
  5. Add @DslMarker (Q241). Make entry points inline only if you accept the ABI coupling (see the inline section).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// 1. Output model (immutable)
data class Request(val url: String, val method: String, val headers: Map<String, String>, val query: Map<String, String>)

// 2-3. Builders
class HeadersBuilder {
    internal val map = linkedMapOf<String, String>()
    infix fun String.to(value: String) { map[this] = value }   // member extension: only usable here
}

class RequestBuilder(private val url: String) {
    var method: String = "GET"
    private val headers = HeadersBuilder()
    private val query = linkedMapOf<String, String>()

    fun headers(block: HeadersBuilder.() -> Unit) { headers.block() }
    fun param(name: String, value: Any) { query[name] = value.toString() }

    internal fun build(): Request {
        require(url.startsWith("https://")) { "Only https allowed: $url" }
        return Request(url, method, headers.map.toMap(), query.toMap())
    }
}

// 4. Entry point
fun request(url: String, block: RequestBuilder.() -> Unit): Request =
    RequestBuilder(url).apply(block).build()

val r = request("https://api.example.com/search") {
    method = "POST"
    param("q", "kotlin")
    param("page", 2)
    headers {
        "Accept" to "application/json"     // HeadersBuilder's member `to`, NOT kotlin.to
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Returning the mutable builder instead of an immutable result, which lets callers keep mutating "built" objects.
  • Leaking the builder by storing this from inside the lambda in a field. The builder then outlives construction.
  • Overusing member extensions like the to above. It shadows kotlin.to inside that scope, which is clever but surprising, so use it deliberately and document it.
  • Making required fields lateinit var on the builder. They fail at runtime instead of compile time. Put required values in the entry function's parameters (request(url) { ... }).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can a Java caller use this DSL? → Yes, but awkwardly. It passes a Function1<RequestBuilder, Unit> and has to return Unit.INSTANCE. Offer a fun interface/Consumer overload or a classic builder for Java.
  2. Should request be inline? → It saves one lambda object per call, which is negligible for config code. In a public library it puts the body into callers' bytecode, so you can't change it without recompiling them. Usually don't, unless it's a hot path or you need reified.
  3. How does buildList infer its type with no type argument? → Builder inference. The compiler infers the type parameter from calls such as add(1) inside the lambda, which is enabled for functions whose lambda parameter has a receiver involving the type variable.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "apply with this". A senior explains the Function1 lowering, the immutable-output versus mutable-builder split, how the structure is enforced by receiver types, putting required fields in entry-point parameters, Java interop and the inline/ABI trade-off.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A navigation-config DSL returned its mutable builders. A feature module mutated a shared route's arguments at runtime, which broke deep links in a completely different feature.

questions.promptHtml: What problem does @DslMarker solve and how does it work? What can still go wrong with it in place?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Without it, nested DSLs compile code that silently calls the outer builder. Knowing @DslMarker separates someone who has designed a DSL from someone who has only used one.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: In nested lambdas with receiver, every outer receiver stays implicitly in scope. So inside tr { } I can accidentally call table.tr() or html.head() without a qualifier, and it compiles. @DslMarker is a meta-annotation. I create my own annotation, mark it @DslMarker, and put it on my builder classes. When more than one implicit receiver carries the same marker, only the innermost one can be used implicitly. Calling an outer one becomes a compile error unless I write this@outer.foo() on purpose. It only restricts implicit receivers. Explicit qualification, top-level functions and other markers still work.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Declaration: @DslMarker annotation class HtmlDsl, then @HtmlDsl class Table, @HtmlDsl class Tr, and so on. A common pattern is to put it on a shared base class or interface (@HtmlDsl abstract class Tag). The marker is inherited, so you can't forget a subclass.
  • Rule: when resolving an implicit receiver call, if the receiver's type, or one of its supertypes, carries a marker that a closer implicit receiver also carries, that outer receiver is skipped. The error tells you to use an explicit receiver.
  • The marker can also be applied to a function type, for example block: (@HtmlDsl Tr).() -> Unit, when you don't own the receiver class.
  • What still compiles:
    • this@table.tr { }, which is explicit and therefore intentional.
    • Calls to receivers with a different marker or no marker. Mixing two DSLs leaves gaps.
    • Top-level functions and extension functions on unmarked types.
    • Calls on an outer builder captured in a local variable, for example val outer = this and then outer.tr().
  • Real-world uses: Compose's RowScope/ColumnScope/BoxScope are annotated @LayoutScopeMarker, which is itself a @DslMarker. That's why Modifier.weight() from an outer Row doesn't resolve inside a nested Box. Kotlin's HTML DSL (kotlinx.html) and Ktor use the same mechanism.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@DslMarker
annotation class MenuDsl

@MenuDsl
abstract class MenuNode

class MenuBuilder : MenuNode() {
    val items = mutableListOf<Item>()
    fun item(title: String, block: ItemBuilder.() -> Unit = {}) {
        items += ItemBuilder(title).apply(block).build()
    }
}

class ItemBuilder(private val title: String) : MenuNode() {
    private val children = mutableListOf<Item>()
    var icon: Int = 0
    fun subItem(title: String) { children += Item(title, 0, emptyList()) }
    fun build() = Item(title, icon, children.toList())
}

data class Item(val title: String, val icon: Int, val children: List<Item>)

fun menu(block: MenuBuilder.() -> Unit) = MenuBuilder().apply(block).items.toList()

val m = menu {
    item("Settings") {
        subItem("Account")
        // item("Logout")          // compile error: MenuBuilder is an outer @MenuDsl receiver
        // this@menu.item("Logout") // compiles: the lambda gets the implicit label @menu; explicit = intentional
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Annotating only some builder classes. The marker has to be on every receiver type in the hierarchy, which is why a common base class helps.
  • Believing @DslMarker restricts properties declared in the outer lambda's body (local vals). It doesn't. It only affects implicit receivers.
  • Using two markers across modules that are meant to nest, for example a design-system DSL inside a screen DSL. Each has its own marker, so the outer one leaks back in.
  • Expecting it to make the DSL immutable or thread-safe. It's purely a name-resolution rule at compile time and has no runtime effect.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does @DslMarker cost anything at runtime? → No. It's a compile-time rule and nothing in the bytecode changes behaviour.
  2. Why can't you call Modifier.weight() inside a Box that's inside a Row? → weight is a member extension of RowScope, and RowScope and BoxScope share @LayoutScopeMarker. With the inner BoxScope in scope, the outer RowScope receiver is blocked.
  3. How do you allow one specific outer call intentionally? → Qualify it with a label (this@item), or expose it as a top-level or unmarked function.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "it prevents calling outer functions". A senior explains the exact rule (same marker, implicit receivers only, innermost wins), lists the escape hatches that still compile, recommends a marked base type, and cites Compose's @LayoutScopeMarker as the production example.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A settings-screen DSL without a marker let item("Logout") written inside a sub-menu register at the top level. The bug shipped because it compiled and looked right in code review. Adding the marker produced 14 compile errors across the codebase, each one a latent misplacement.

questions.subtopic: Gradle Kotlin DSL & Compose as DSLs
questions.promptHtml: Gradle Kotlin DSL and Jetpack Compose are both described as Kotlin DSLs. Which language features actually make them work, and where do those features cause pain?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Every Android developer uses both daily. A senior should be able to explain why android { } autocompletes, why accessors sometimes "don't exist", and why Modifier.align only works in certain scopes.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Gradle Kotlin DSL is mostly lambdas with receiver. android { ... } is a generated extension function on Project that configures the android extension. Gradle's Java Action<T> interfaces behave as if they had a receiver because the kotlin-dsl setup applies the SAM-with-receiver compiler plugin. The type-safe accessors (android, implementation(...), libs.xyz) are generated, and only for plugins applied in the plugins {} block. Compose is different. Composables are plain functions transformed by the Compose compiler plugin. The DSL feel comes from trailing lambdas, and layout scopes (RowScope, ColumnScope, BoxScope) are lambdas with receiver carrying a @DslMarker (@LayoutScopeMarker). That's why Modifier.weight only resolves inside a Row or Column.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Gradle Kotlin DSL:

Feature What it does
Generated type-safe accessors Gradle inspects the plugins applied in plugins {} and generates extensions like Project.android(configure: ApplicationExtension.() -> Unit) and DependencyHandler.implementation(...).
SAM-with-receiver Gradle APIs take Action<T>, which is annotated @HasImplicitReceiver. The Kotlin DSL compiles scripts with the sam-with-receiver plugin, so tasks.register("x") { group = "y" } sees the Task as this, not it.
Delegated properties val myTask by tasks.registering { }, val ext by extra(...).
Version catalogs libs.androidx.core.ktx is a generated accessor tree built from libs.versions.toml.

Pain points:

  • If a plugin is applied with apply(plugin = "...") or from allprojects {}, no accessors are generated. You fall back to configure<ApplicationExtension> { } or extensions.getByType<...>().
  • Generating accessors is part of script compilation. Kotlin scripts compile more slowly than Groovy on first configuration, so configuration-cache and build-logic convention plugins (build-logic included build) matter at scale.
  • In convention plugins written as plain Kotlin classes, you don't get script accessors at all. You use the typed APIs directly.

Compose:

Feature Role
Trailing lambdas Column { Text("a") } is just Column(content = { ... }).
Compose compiler plugin Rewrites @Composable functions to take a Composer and change flags. That's what makes UI declarative. It's a compiler transform, not a DSL feature. The plugin moved into the Kotlin repo with Kotlin 2.0.
Lambdas with receiver content: @Composable RowScope.() -> Unit. RowScope contributes Modifier.weight() and Modifier.align(Alignment.Vertical).
@LayoutScopeMarker (@DslMarker) Stops an outer RowScope from leaking into a nested Box, so scope-specific modifiers can't be misapplied.
Member extensions fun Modifier.weight(...) declared inside RowScope, so it only exists where that receiver is in scope.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// build.gradle.kts
plugins {
    id("com.android.application")      // accessors for `android {}` are generated because of this
    kotlin("android")
}

android {                              // Project.android(ApplicationExtension.() -> Unit)
    namespace = "com.example.app"
    defaultConfig { minSdk = 24 }
}

tasks.register("printVersion") {       // Action<Task> with implicit receiver: `this` is Task
    doLast { println(project.version) }
}
@Composable
fun Toolbar() {
    Row {
        Text("Title", modifier = Modifier.weight(1f))           // RowScope member extension
        Box {
            // Text("x", Modifier.weight(1f))                     // does not compile: RowScope blocked by @LayoutScopeMarker
            Text("x", Modifier.align(Alignment.Center))          // BoxScope.align
        }
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Copy-pasting android { } into a script where the plugin is applied imperatively, then "fixing" the unresolved reference with string-based APIs instead of applying the plugin in plugins {}.
  • Assuming Compose @Composable lambdas are ordinary lambdas with receiver. The receiver is a scope, and the composability is a separate compiler transform.
  • Passing a RowScope receiver down to a child composable as a parameter to "escape" the marker. That works, but it couples the child to its parent layout. Prefer passing a Modifier built at the call site.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does tasks.register("x") { } give this but plain Kotlin code calling a Java Consumer<T> gives it? → Gradle's Action is marked @HasImplicitReceiver, and the sam-with-receiver plugin honours that annotation. Normal SAM conversion passes the argument as it.
  2. How do you write a Compose API that only works inside your own container? → Define @LayoutScopeMarker interface MyScope { fun Modifier.pinned(): Modifier } and take content: @Composable MyScope.() -> Unit.
  3. How would you speed up a 300-module Kotlin DSL build? → Move shared logic into convention plugins in an included build, enable the configuration cache, avoid allprojects/subprojects blocks, and keep scripts thin so accessor generation and script compilation are cached.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "android {} is a lambda". A senior names the specific mechanisms (generated accessors tied to plugins {}, sam-with-receiver via @HasImplicitReceiver, member extensions in layout scopes, @LayoutScopeMarker) and knows that Compose's real magic is a compiler plugin, not the DSL.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: After migrating from Groovy, a large project's subprojects { android { } } stopped compiling because no accessors exist there. The team replaced it with convention plugins, which also cut configuration time noticeably.

questions.promptHtml: What are Kotlin contracts? Explain callsInPlace and returns(...) implies ..., what they let the compiler do, their stability and opt-in status, and the risk of writing your own.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Contracts explain why require(x != null) smart-casts x and why you can assign a val inside run { }. Writing them is a trust contract with the compiler, and seniors are expected to know it isn't verified.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A contract is a statement a function makes to the compiler's data-flow analysis about its behaviour, declared in a contract { } block as the first statement of the body. callsInPlace(block, InvocationKind.EXACTLY_ONCE) says the lambda runs during the call, a known number of times, and doesn't escape. That's why you can initialise a val inside run { }. returns() implies (x != null) or returns(true) implies (x is Foo) tell the compiler what's true after the call returns, so callers get smart casts, as with require, check and isNullOrEmpty. Declaring contracts needs @OptIn(ExperimentalContracts::class) and is still experimental. Callers don't need to opt in. The critical part: the compiler mostly trusts contracts without proving them, so a wrong contract gives you an NPE or ClassCastException with no !! anywhere in sight.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Effects you can declare:

Effect Meaning What callers gain
callsInPlace(f, EXACTLY_ONCE) f runs exactly once before the function returns Definite assignment of val in f; initialisation analysis
callsInPlace(f, AT_LEAST_ONCE) runs ≥1 times var definitely assigned after the call
callsInPlace(f, AT_MOST_ONCE) runs 0 or 1 times val assignment allowed (no reassignment), not definite
callsInPlace(f) (UNKNOWN) runs in place, any count Smart casts from outside remain stable inside the lambda
returns() implies cond if the function returns normally, cond holds Smart cast after require/check-style calls
returns(true/false/null) implies cond if it returns that value, cond holds Smart cast in if (x.isValid())
returnsNotNull() implies cond if it returns non-null, cond holds Smart cast inside ?.let / if (r != null)

Constraints (as of Kotlin 2.x; check the API reference for your exact version):

  • contract { } must be the first statement of a function with a block body.
  • Conditions are limited to is checks, == null/!= null on parameters or the receiver, and boolean parameters combined with &&, || and !. You can't call arbitrary functions in a condition.
  • They aren't allowed on members that can be overridden (open, abstract, interface members). An override could break the promise.
  • Contracts are stored in Kotlin metadata, so they work across module and library boundaries.

Stdlib examples you rely on every day:

require(value)            -> returns() implies value
requireNotNull(x)         -> returns() implies (x != null)
String?.isNullOrEmpty()   -> returns(false) implies (this != null)
run / let / apply / also / with -> callsInPlace(block, EXACTLY_ONCE)

Status and version notes:

  • Contracts were introduced in Kotlin 1.3 and are still Experimental. Declaring one requires @OptIn(kotlin.contracts.ExperimentalContracts::class).
  • Kotlin 2.2.20 added further Experimental extensions, each behind a compiler flag: generics in contract type assertions and contracts in property getters and some operator functions (-Xallow-contracts-on-more-functions), returnsNotNull() (-Xallow-condition-implies-returns-contracts) and holdsIn, which says a condition holds inside a lambda (-Xallow-holdsin-contract). returnsNotNull and holdsIn additionally require @OptIn(ExperimentalExtendedContracts::class). Treat all of these as unstable for library APIs. I'd check the "What's new" page for any release after 2.2.20 before claiming they're stable.

Verification: the compiler doesn't prove that returns(true) implies (x != null) is true of your implementation. It takes your word for it. There are some diagnostics around in-place lambdas, for example warnings when a lambda declared in-place is passed somewhere it could escape, but the implication logic isn't checked. Callers compile smart casts with no runtime null check, so the failure appears at the use site, far from the lie.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import kotlin.contracts.ExperimentalContracts
import kotlin.contracts.InvocationKind
import kotlin.contracts.contract

@OptIn(ExperimentalContracts::class)
fun String?.isPresent(): Boolean {
    contract { returns(true) implies (this@isPresent != null) }
    return !this.isNullOrBlank()
}

@OptIn(ExperimentalContracts::class)
inline fun <T> measured(tag: String, block: () -> T): T {
    contract { callsInPlace(block, InvocationKind.EXACTLY_ONCE) }
    val start = System.nanoTime()
    try { return block() } finally { android.util.Log.d(tag, "${(System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000_000} ms") }
}

fun use(token: String?) {
    if (token.isPresent()) println(token.length)   // smart cast, no `!!`

    val config: String
    measured("load") { config = "loaded" }         // allowed: EXACTLY_ONCE
    println(config)
}

// WRONG: lies to the compiler. Block posted to a Handler runs later, not in place.
@OptIn(ExperimentalContracts::class)
fun onMain(handler: android.os.Handler, block: () -> Unit) {
    contract { callsInPlace(block, InvocationKind.EXACTLY_ONCE) }   // false promise
    handler.post(block)
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Declaring callsInPlace on a function that stores or posts the lambda. It's a lie, and it permits reading a val that hasn't been assigned yet.
  • Refactoring a function's body (flipping a boolean, adding an early return) without updating the contract. Nothing fails at compile time.
  • Using contracts in a published library API without telling consumers they're experimental. A future compiler could change the semantics, and the opt-in exists for exactly that reason.
  • Expecting contracts to work on open members or interface methods. They're rejected there.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Do callers need @OptIn? → No. Only the declaring function does. Callers silently benefit, and that's why bad contracts spread.
  2. Does callsInPlace require the function to be inline? → No, but in practice in-place lambdas are usually inline. If it isn't inline, the lambda object still exists and the contract only affects analysis.
  3. How would you protect a codebase from wrong contracts? → Keep them in a small, owned core module, unit-test each implies branch (null, non-null, both return values), add a lint or detekt rule that flags contract { outside the allowlisted module, and require a second reviewer for contract changes.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "contracts help smart casts". A senior lists the effects and what each enables, the constraints, the stdlib functions that rely on them, the Experimental opt-in and the 2.2.20 additions, and stresses that the compiler doesn't verify them, so they're a trusted, unchecked promise.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A "helper" with returns(false) implies (this != null) went wrong after a refactor flipped its logic. Callers kept their smart casts and crashed with an NPE on .length (see Q246).

questions.contextHtml:
Your app (3.1M MAU) has an internal deep-link DSL in :core:navigation. After release 8.4, analytics show that 11% of /product/{id}/reviews links land on the home fallback instead of the reviews screen. Product-detail links work. The release also bumped AGP and changed an <intent-filter> in the manifest. QA says links work "most of the time". Here's the DSL and its usage:

class DeepLinkConfig { val patterns = mutableListOf<String>() }

class HostBuilder(private val host: String, private val config: DeepLinkConfig) {
    fun path(pattern: String, block: PathBuilder.() -> Unit = {}) {
        val builder = PathBuilder("https://$host$pattern", config)
        config.patterns += builder.base
        builder.block()
    }
}

class PathBuilder(val base: String, private val config: DeepLinkConfig) {
    fun child(segment: String) { config.patterns += "$base$segment" }
}

fun deepLinks(block: DeepLinkConfig.() -> Unit) = DeepLinkConfig().apply(block)
fun DeepLinkConfig.host(name: String, block: HostBuilder.() -> Unit) = HostBuilder(name, this).block()

val links = deepLinks {
    host("shop.example.com") {
        path("/product/{id}") {
            path("/reviews")          // added in 8.4
            child("/questions")
        }
    }
}

The "most of the time" comes from the fact that some users open review links through a web fallback that has its own matcher.
questions.promptHtml: Find the bug, explain why it compiled, and fix it so this whole class of bug can't happen again.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "The manifest intent-filter is wrong," or "AGP broke deep links." Or they spot that /reviews is wrong but fix only that line by changing it to child("/reviews"), without explaining why the compiler accepted it or preventing the next one.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask:
    • Which patterns are actually registered at runtime? I'd dump links.patterns. This separates a DSL bug from a manifest bug.
    • Did the manifest change touch the /product path prefix? That decides whether the red herring is real.
    • Do review links that fail share a format, for example no trailing slash? That checks for a matching bug versus a registration bug.
    • Is the 11% tied to app-link verification (autoVerify) on some OEMs? That would point to a platform issue rather than code.
  2. Immediate mitigation: Ship a server-side redirect, or a fallback pattern, that maps https://shop.example.com/reviews to the reviews screen while parsing the product id from a query param, if the web side supports it. Then hotfix the DSL usage. Neither needs a full release train.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    1. Inside path("/product/{id}") { }, the call path("/reviews") resolved to the outer HostBuilder.path, because HostBuilder is still an implicit receiver. It registered https://shop.example.com/reviews, not /product/{id}/reviews. That fits "only nested links are broken".
    2. The manifest <intent-filter> change removed pathPrefix="/product". That's possible, but then product links would break too, and they don't.
    3. App-link verification failing on some devices. That would affect all links equally, not just reviews.
  4. How I'd verify each:
    • A unit test asserting links.patterns contains https://shop.example.com/product/{id}/reviews. It fails today, and the actual list shows https://shop.example.com/reviews.
    • adb shell am start -a android.intent.action.VIEW -d "https://shop.example.com/product/12/reviews" on a debug build, with logging in the router.
    • adb shell pm get-app-links <package> to check verification state, which rules out hypothesis 3.
    • In the IDE, Ctrl+click on path("/reviews") jumps to HostBuilder.path. That's the proof.
  5. Root cause: Lambdas with receiver nest their implicit receivers. Inside PathBuilder.() -> Unit, both PathBuilder (inner) and HostBuilder (outer) are implicit receivers. PathBuilder has no path member, so resolution walks outward and finds HostBuilder.path. That's perfectly legal Kotlin, so it compiled and passed review because it reads naturally.
  6. Fix: Short term: change the call to child("/reviews") and add the regression test. Long term: add a @DslMarker so outer receivers can't be used implicitly, and give PathBuilder real nesting. 
    @DslMarker annotation class DeepLinkDsl

@DeepLinkDsl class DeepLinkConfig { internal val patterns = mutableListOf<String>() }

@DeepLinkDsl
class HostBuilder(private val host: String, private val config: DeepLinkConfig) {
    fun path(pattern: String, block: PathBuilder.() -> Unit = {}) {
        PathBuilder("https://$host$pattern", config).apply { register() }.block()
    }
}

@DeepLinkDsl
class PathBuilder(private val base: String, private val config: DeepLinkConfig) {
    internal fun register() { config.patterns += base }
    fun path(segment: String, block: PathBuilder.() -> Unit = {}) {   // nested paths are explicit now
        PathBuilder("$base$segment", config).apply { register() }.block()
    }
}

fun deepLinks(block: DeepLinkConfig.() -> Unit): List<String> =
    DeepLinkConfig().apply(block).patterns.toList()            // return immutable result
fun DeepLinkConfig.host(name: String, block: HostBuilder.() -> Unit) = HostBuilder(name, this).block()
    With the marker in place, any remaining implicit outer calls become compile errors. I'd fix each one deliberately.
  7. Prevention:
    • A golden test that snapshots the full registered pattern list and is reviewed on change.
    • A test that cross-checks every DSL pattern against the merged manifest's intent filters.
    • A review checklist item: every builder class in a DSL carries the marker, ideally through a marked base type.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why):
    • I wouldn't roll back AGP or the manifest. The evidence doesn't point there.
    • I wouldn't replace the DSL with stringly-typed config. The DSL is fine once it's scoped.
    • Adding the marker is a source-breaking change for every module using the DSL. In a monorepo that's what we want. For an external SDK I'd ship it in a minor release with release notes.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if PathBuilder and HostBuilder live in different modules owned by different teams? → The marker annotation must be shared, so put it in the DSL core module. Different markers don't block each other.
  • What if someone really needs a host-level path from inside a path block? → They write this@host.path(...), which is explicit, reviewable and intentional.
  • Could the compiler have warned without @DslMarker? → No. Implicit receiver resolution walking outward is the specified behaviour.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: On a menu DSL, adding @DslMarker turned up 14 compile errors across 9 modules. Each one was a misregistered item that had been in production for months, mostly unnoticed because the misplaced items were rarely used.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames the manifest or AGP, or can't explain why it compiled.
  • Hire: finds the outer-receiver resolution, fixes the call and adds a test.
  • Strong hire: explains implicit receiver nesting, applies @DslMarker through a marked base type, returns immutable output, sets up golden or manifest tests, and treats the marker as a deliberate source-breaking migration.

questions.contextHtml:
You own the analytics SDK used by 3 apps and about 60 engineers. There are 420 event types today, and roughly 25 new events land each sprint. 30% of call sites are in legacy Java modules. Data science reports that 6% of events arrive missing required fields (screen, userTier), and 2% have keys with typos. A staff engineer proposes a Kotlin DSL:

track("checkout_started") {
    screen = "cart"
    prop("items", 3)
    prop("value_inr", 1299)
}

Another engineer wants generated data classes per event from a schema (CheckoutStarted(screen, items, valueInr).track()). The SDK is published as a binary artifact, and the apps update it on different schedules.
questions.promptHtml: Which API do you ship and why? Cover required-field safety, Java interop, binary compatibility and performance.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "A DSL looks cleaner, let's do it," or "DSLs are slow." Either way the answer ignores the actual failure mode: required fields can't be enforced at compile time inside a free-form receiver lambda, and 30% of callers are in Java.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask:
    • Is there a single source of truth for event schemas? A schema is what makes code generation possible.
    • How tolerant is the pipeline to new optional properties? That tells me how often the API surface will change.
    • What's the Java call-site trend? If Java is shrinking fast, I'd optimise for Kotlin and give Java a basic path.
    • Are events fired in hot paths like scroll or impression tracking? That determines whether allocation matters.
    • How far behind can apps lag on SDK versions? That sets the binary-compatibility bar.
  2. Immediate mitigation: Before any redesign, add runtime validation in track() against the schema. In debug builds, throw on a missing required field. In release builds, drop and count invalid events. That stops the 6% from polluting dashboards this sprint.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (options evaluated):
    Option Required fields Typos in keys Java callers Binary compat Verdict
    Free-form DSL (prop("k", v)) Runtime only (lateinit/check in build) Still possible Awkward (Function1 + return Unit.INSTANCE) Fine if not inline Doesn't fix the reported bugs
    Hand-written data classes + named args Compile time (constructor params) Impossible (properties) Good (constructors) Adding a param breaks callers unless defaults plus @JvmOverloads Good, but 420 classes by hand
    Schema-generated event classes Compile time Impossible Good Generator controls evolution Primary API
    Hybrid DSL: required params in the call, optionals in the lambda Compile time for required Typed optionals OK with a Java overload Fine Good for ad-hoc events
  4. How I'd verify each:
    • Prototype both APIs on 20 real events and measure call-site diffs and errors caught.
    • Run Kotlin's binary-compatibility-validator plugin (apiDump/apiCheck) on the SDK to see how each design changes the public ABI.
    • Write a Java sample module in CI to check usability from Java.
    • Microbenchmark track() with Jetpack Microbenchmark to confirm allocation per event is irrelevant (one lambda plus a map is roughly hundreds of bytes, which is noise next to the JSON serialisation and disk write).
  5. Root cause (of the current bugs): Stringly-typed, optional-by-default APIs. A DSL keeps that shape: screen = ... inside a receiver lambda is a mutable property that callers can forget, and prop("vaule_inr", ...) still compiles. A DSL changes the syntax but not the type safety.
  6. Fix: Primary: generate event classes from the schema, with required properties as non-null constructor params and optionals defaulted. Secondary: keep a small hybrid DSL for experiments, with required data as real parameters. 
    // generated
class CheckoutStarted(
    val screen: Screen,                  // enum, not String
    val userTier: UserTier,
    val items: Int,
    val valueInr: Long,
    val coupon: String? = null,
) : AnalyticsEvent {
    override val name get() = "checkout_started"
    override fun props() = mapOf("screen" to screen.key, "user_tier" to userTier.key,
        "items" to items, "value_inr" to valueInr, "coupon" to coupon)
}

// hybrid DSL for ad-hoc events: required fields are parameters, not lambda properties
@DslMarker annotation class EventDsl
@EventDsl class PropsBuilder internal constructor() {
    internal val map = linkedMapOf<String, Any?>()
    infix fun String.setTo(value: Any?) { map[this] = value }
}
fun Analytics.experiment(name: String, screen: Screen, props: PropsBuilder.() -> Unit = {}) =
    send(name, mapOf("screen" to screen.key) + PropsBuilder().apply(props).map)

// Java-friendly entry point instead of forcing Function1/Unit.INSTANCE on Java callers.
// Distinct name avoids overload ambiguity for Kotlin lambdas.
fun interface PropsConfigurer { fun configure(builder: PropsBuilder) }
fun Analytics.experimentWith(name: String, screen: Screen, props: PropsConfigurer) =
    experiment(name, screen) { props.configure(this) }
    Binary compatibility: I'd keep public entry points non-inline, because inline bodies are copied into app bytecode and changing them requires recompiling callers. I'd run binary-compatibility-validator in CI. Generated classes add optional fields with defaults, so Kotlin callers are source-compatible. For Java constructor compatibility I'd generate @JvmOverloads or use a static factory. Adding a parameter to a data class constructor is a binary break for already-compiled callers, so the generator must emit overloads.
  7. Prevention:
    • A CI step fails if an event in code isn't in the schema registry.
    • Release builds track the invalid-event counter as a metric, with an alert above 0.5%.
    • A lint rule bans raw send(name, map) outside the SDK.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why):
    • I wouldn't ship the free-form DSL as the primary API. It's pleasant to write but fixes neither reported bug.
    • I wouldn't make the entry points inline to "save a lambda". The saving is a few bytes per event, and the ABI lock-in lasts for the lifetime of the SDK.
    • I wouldn't use reflection-based validation at runtime. It costs startup time and needs kotlin-reflect.
    • I accept the cost of maintaining a code generator, because 420+ events with weekly growth justifies it.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if there's no schema registry and leadership won't fund one? → Hand-write sealed event classes for the top 50 events (likely most of the volume), and use the hybrid DSL with runtime validation for the long tail.
  • What if events fire on every scroll frame (impressions)? → Batch them. Use a pre-sized buffer object pool or primitive-keyed records instead of a map per event. At that point the DSL's allocation does matter, so measure it with the allocation tracker.
  • Should Screen be an enum or a sealed interface? → An enum if the set is closed in the SDK. A sealed interface or value class if each app defines its own screens, because enums can't be extended across modules.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team shipped a beautiful event DSL. Six months later, missing-field rates were unchanged, because the DSL made every field optional by construction. The schema-generated classes that replaced it dropped invalid events to near zero within two releases.

• No hire: picks based on looks, or claims DSLs are slow without numbers.
  • Hire: sees that the DSL doesn't enforce required fields, puts required data in parameters, and considers Java callers.
  • Strong hire: compares the options against the actual failure data, separates syntax from type safety, addresses binary compatibility (inline ABI, constructor params, @JvmOverloads, binary-compatibility-validator), offers a Java fun interface overload, and adds runtime validation as immediate mitigation.

questions.contextHtml:
Release 7.3 goes to 1.2M DAU. Crash-free users drop from 99.92% to 99.41% within 24 hours. The top Crashlytics issue is new:

java.lang.NullPointerException: Attempt to invoke virtual method 'int java.lang.String.length()' on a null object reference
    at com.example.auth.SessionHeaderInterceptor.intercept(SessionHeaderInterceptor.kt:31)
    at okhttp3.internal.http.RealInterceptorChain.proceed(RealInterceptorChain.kt:109)

Line 31 is if (!token.isMissing()) builder.header("X-Len", token.length.toString()). There's no !! anywhere in the file. The release also upgraded OkHttp 4.12 to 5.x (a red herring) and the crashes skew towards Android 14 devices (also a red herring: those users simply updated first). git blame shows a "cleanup" PR in :core:common that renamed and reimplemented a helper:

@OptIn(ExperimentalContracts::class)
fun String?.isMissing(): Boolean {
    contract { returns(false) implies (this@isMissing != null) }
    return this?.isBlank() ?: false        // was: this == null || this.isBlank()
}
questions.promptHtml: Walk me through the investigation, the root cause, the fix, and how you'd stop it happening again.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add !! or ?.," or "Roll back OkHttp because the interceptor is in the trace." Or "It's an Android 14 bug." None of these explains how Kotlin's null safety let this through.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask:
    • What share of sessions have a null token at that point? For example logged-out users or the pre-login warm-up call. That explains why some users crash and others don't.
    • Did the crash appear in the internal or beta build? That tells me whether the test matrix covers logged-out flows.
    • Is the crash tied to the 7.3 binary only? I'd check by version in Crashlytics, which rules the OS in or out.
    • Which other call sites use isMissing()? That defines the blast radius.
  2. Immediate mitigation:
    • Halt the staged rollout in the Play Console.
    • If a remote flag exists, disable the pre-login prefetch that sends requests with no token. That stops most of the crashes.
    • Prepare a hotfix for isMissing() itself. A single function fixes every call site.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    1. The contract is now false. The new body returns false for null (null?.isBlank() is null, and ?: false gives false), while the contract tells the compiler that false means non-null. Callers smart-cast token to String with no runtime check, so .length crashes. The diff, the line and "no !!" all fit.
    2. The OkHttp 5 upgrade changed interceptor threading or order. But the NPE is on our own String.length(), not inside OkHttp.
    3. Android 14 behaviour. The distribution by OS matches the adoption curve for 7.3, not a platform change.
  4. How I'd verify each:
    • A unit test: assertTrue(null.isMissing()). It fails with the new body, so the bug reproduces in milliseconds.
    • Show Kotlin Bytecode on the interceptor: there's no Intrinsics.checkNotNull and a direct String.length() call after isMissing() returns false. That proves the smart cast came from the contract.
    • Crashlytics custom keys or breadcrumbs: logged_in=false on 100% of the crashes.
    • For OkHttp: reproduce with a null token on 7.2's OkHttp version plus the new helper. It still crashes, which rules OkHttp out.
  5. Root cause: Contracts are trusted, not verified. The refactor changed the null branch from true to false but kept returns(false) implies (this != null). Data-flow analysis in every caller assumes token != null in the !isMissing() branch and emits a plain virtual call. Kotlin's null-safety checks only run at boundaries (Java interop, !!, platform types). There's nothing at a smart cast, so the NPE lands at the use site, far from the bug.
  6. Fix: Short term: restore the correct semantics in the helper and add exhaustive tests. 
    @OptIn(ExperimentalContracts::class)
fun String?.isMissing(): Boolean {
    contract { returns(false) implies (this@isMissing != null) }
    return this == null || this.isBlank()
}

class IsMissingTest {
    @Test fun nullIsMissing() = assertTrue(null.isMissing())
    @Test fun blankIsMissing() = assertTrue("  ".isMissing())
    @Test fun valueIsPresent() = assertFalse("abc".isMissing())
}
    Long term: delete custom contracts that only duplicate the stdlib. token.isNullOrBlank() already has a correct, maintained contract (returns(false) implies (this != null)). The best custom contract is the one you don't write.
  7. Prevention:
    • A detekt or lint rule (a simple ForbiddenImport on kotlin.contracts.contract, or a custom rule) that allows contracts only in an allowlisted file or module, with CODEOWNERS on that module.
    • A policy that every function with a contract has a test per implies branch: null, non-null, and each declared return value.
    • Staged rollout gates on crash-free users (halt below 99.8% at 5% rollout), which would have contained this to about 60k users instead of everyone.
    • Release-build crash dashboards keyed by app version so OS-skew red herrings are obvious.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why):
    • I wouldn't sprinkle ?./!! at call sites. That hides the root cause and leaves the other call sites broken.
    • I wouldn't roll back OkHttp. The evidence clears it, and a rollback reintroduces risk.
    • I wouldn't ban contracts outright if the team genuinely needs a domain-specific returns implies. I'd concentrate and test them instead.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the lie were callsInPlace(block, EXACTLY_ONCE) on a function that posts block to a Handler? → The caller can declare val x: String and assign it inside the lambda, then read x immediately. On the JVM the captured val is a Ref.ObjectRef whose field is still null, so you get a null in a "non-null" String, a crash, or a wrong default for primitives. Same class of bug: trusted, unverified analysis.
  • Would K2 have caught this? → No. The contract's implication about the function body isn't checked by K1 or K2.
  • The helper is in a library module consumed as a binary. Do callers pick up the fixed contract automatically? → The contract is in the library's metadata, so callers get whatever contract was present when they compiled. Here the contract text was right all along, and only the body changed. Shipping the fixed body is enough, but the apps need the new artifact.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team had 11 hand-written contract helpers. An audit found 2 of them wrong for blank strings. Both were replaced with stdlib functions, and the remaining contracts moved into one file with 100% branch tests and CODEOWNERS.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: adds !!/?., blames OkHttp or Android 14, and can't explain why Kotlin allowed it.
  • Hire: identifies the contract and body mismatch, fixes the helper and adds tests.
  • Strong hire: explains that smart casts from contracts carry no runtime check, verifies through bytecode and a unit test, halts the rollout, prefers stdlib functions, restricts contracts with lint and CODEOWNERS, and connects it to the callsInPlace variant.

questions.contextHtml:
A trading-style chart (a custom View, not Compose) draws 4,000 points per series, 3 series, at 60 fps during pan and zoom. Code review loved the operator-based geometry:

data class Vec(val x: Float, val y: Float) {
    operator fun plus(o: Vec) = Vec(x + o.x, y + o.y)
    operator fun minus(o: Vec) = Vec(x - o.x, y - o.y)
    operator fun times(s: Float) = Vec(x * s, y * s)
}

override fun onDraw(canvas: Canvas) {
    for (series in seriesList) {
        val screen = series.points.map { (it - viewport.origin) * scale + padding }   // List<Vec>
        for ((a, b) in screen.zipWithNext()) canvas.drawLine(a.x, a.y, b.x, b.y, paint)
    }
}

On a mid-range device (Snapdragon 6-series, 4 GB RAM), the macrobenchmark FrameTimingMetric shows a p50 frame time of 11 ms, a p95 of 27 ms and a p99 of 41 ms while panning. The Perfetto trace shows frequent HeapTaskDaemon concurrent GC slices overlapping frames. Someone suggests switching to SurfaceView and hardware layers (a red herring for this symptom).
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose this and optimise it while keeping the code readable. What do operators cost, and what would you change?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Operators are slow, remove them," or "Move drawing to a background thread / SurfaceView." The operators aren't slow. The allocations they hide are what hurts, and threading doesn't fix GC pressure.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask:
    • Is the jank only during pan and zoom, or also when static? That tells me whether per-frame recomputation is the problem.
    • What's the minimum device tier we support? That sets the budget: 16.6 ms at 60 Hz, 8.3 ms at 120 Hz.
    • Do the points change every frame, or only the viewport transform? That decides whether results can be cached.
    • Is points a List<Vec> coming from the repository? That tells me whether the storage format can change.
  2. Immediate mitigation: Hoist the computation out of onDraw and cache screen coordinates. Recompute them only when the viewport changes, not on every invalidate caused by unrelated redraws such as the crosshair.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    1. Allocation churn from operators and collection operators. Per series per frame: minus, times and plus each allocate a Vec, so 3 × 4,000 = 12,000 Vecs. map adds an ArrayList of 4,000. zipWithNext adds about 4,000 Pairs and another list. Destructuring (a, b) adds nothing. That's about 16,000 objects per series, 48,000 per frame and 2.9M per second at 60 fps. At about 16 bytes per Vec (8-byte object header plus 2 floats on ART) and about 16 bytes per Pair (header plus 2 compressed references), plus the backing arrays, that's roughly 290 KB per series, about 0.9 MB per frame, and about 50 MB/s of garbage. ART's concurrent collector handles a lot, but at that rate it competes with the UI and RenderThreads on a mid-range CPU and causes allocation stalls. This fits the GC slices overlapping frames.
    2. Too many drawLine calls (12,000 per frame). That's a real cost, but drawLines(FloatArray) batches them and it's secondary.
    3. SurfaceView/layers. That would help with compositing, not with GC churn in our own code. It's a red herring.
  4. How I'd verify each:
    • Android Studio Memory Profiler with allocation tracking ("Track all allocations") during a 5 s pan. I'd expect Vec, Pair and ArrayList at the top, with counts in the millions.
    • Perfetto: correlate HeapTaskDaemon and GC slices with Choreographer#doFrame overruns. Then repeat after the fix.
    • Macrobenchmark FrameTimingMetric before and after on the same device, with at least 10 iterations, comparing p95 and p99.
    • Show Kotlin Bytecode on plus to confirm that each operator is a NEW Vec. Operators add no overhead of their own. The allocation is the cost.
  5. Root cause: Operators are only function calls, so a + b costs exactly what plus does. Here plus returns a new heap object. Readable operator chains hide three allocations per point, and functional collection operators (map, zipWithNext) add an intermediate list and a Pair per element, all repeated 60 times a second.
  6. Fix: Short term: precompute into a reusable FloatArray and draw with drawLines. There are no per-frame allocations, and the operators stay where they help readability, outside the hot loop. 
    class SeriesRenderer(capacity: Int) {
    private var buffer = FloatArray(capacity * 4)            // reused across frames

    fun render(canvas: Canvas, xs: FloatArray, ys: FloatArray, count: Int,
               ox: Float, oy: Float, scale: Float, padX: Float, padY: Float, paint: Paint) {
        if (count < 2) return
        val needed = (count - 1) * 4
        if (buffer.size < needed) buffer = FloatArray(needed)
        var prevX = (xs[0] - ox) * scale + padX
        var prevY = (ys[0] - oy) * scale + padY
        var j = 0
        for (i in 1 until count) {                             // intrinsified: no IntRange object
            val x = (xs[i] - ox) * scale + padX
            val y = (ys[i] - oy) * scale + padY
            buffer[j++] = prevX; buffer[j++] = prevY; buffer[j++] = x; buffer[j++] = y
            prevX = x; prevY = y
        }
        canvas.drawLines(buffer, 0, needed, paint)            // one call instead of 3,999
    }
}
    Long term, if we want to keep operator readability in geometry code: model Vec as a value class packing two floats into a Long, which is the approach Compose takes with Offset. The operators then work on a primitive long with no allocation, as long as the value isn't stored as a generic type or nullable. List<Vec> would box every element again, so storage stays in primitive arrays. Value-class boxing rules are covered in the sealed and value classes chunk. 
    @JvmInline value class PackedVec(private val packed: Long) {
    constructor(x: Float, y: Float) : this((x.toRawBits().toLong() shl 32) or (y.toRawBits().toLong() and 0xFFFF_FFFFL))
    val x: Float get() = Float.fromBits((packed shr 32).toInt())
    val y: Float get() = Float.fromBits(packed.toInt())
    operator fun plus(o: PackedVec) = PackedVec(x + o.x, y + o.y)   // no heap allocation when used unboxed
    operator fun times(s: Float) = PackedVec(x * s, y * s)
}
    Expected result (illustrative): allocations during pan drop from millions to roughly zero, and p95 frame time falls from 27 ms to under 12 ms on the same device. I'd confirm it with the benchmark rather than promise it.
  7. Prevention:
    • A macrobenchmark in CI for the chart pan, with an alert on p95 regressions of more than 15%.
    • A code-review guideline: no allocating operators or collection chains inside onDraw, onMeasure, RecyclerView bind or draw lambdas.
    • Optionally, a debug-only check that counts allocations per frame with Debug.startAllocCounting() (deprecated but still usable for spot checks) or the allocation tracker during dev builds.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why):
    • I wouldn't ban operator overloading. Value semantics are great in non-hot code, and value classes keep them cheap.
    • I wouldn't move to SurfaceView or a render thread first. It's a bigger change that doesn't address GC.
    • I wouldn't convert to Sequence. It still allocates the Vecs, and adds iterator and lambda overhead for this size.
    • Mutable Vec with plusAssign would avoid allocation, but shared mutable value objects cause aliasing bugs. I'd only use it as a scratch object local to the renderer.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Does for ((a, b) in pairs) allocate? → Destructuring calls component1()/component2() and allocates nothing by itself. The Pairs were already allocated by zipWithNext.
  • Does x in 0f..width allocate in the hot loop? → Literal Int, Long and Char ranges in in and for are intrinsified. For Float ranges, I'd check the bytecode instead of assuming. Writing x >= 0f && x <= width removes the doubt in a hot loop.
  • What if the data arrives as List<Vec> from the repository and can't change? → Convert once per data update into FloatArrays (O(n), off the main thread), and draw from those. The cost moves from per frame to per data change.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A charting screen's jank was "fixed" twice with hardware layers and frame skipping. The real fix was a 40-line renderer using reused FloatArrays that removed about 2.5M allocations per second. The operator-based Vec API stayed for gesture maths outside the draw loop.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: says operators themselves are slow, or jumps to threading or SurfaceView without profiling.
  • Hire: identifies per-frame allocations from operators and map/zipWithNext, caches the results and uses primitive arrays with drawLines.
  • Strong hire: quantifies the allocations (objects per frame, MB/s), verifies with the allocation tracker, Perfetto and macrobenchmark, explains that operators are just calls, offers value-class packing with its boxing caveat (List<Vec>), and sets up regression benchmarks.
